Why not use ten digits, like we do? Well, it's much easier and more reliable to tell on from off than to tell ten different voltages apart.
Two-state switches are also tiny, cheap and fast. So the new Northern Ireland curriculum puts it simply: computers process everything as binary.

Next, hexadecimal, or hex. It's base sixteen, so it needs sixteen digits: zero to nine, then A to F.
A is ten, B is eleven, all the way up to F, which is fifteen.
The clever bit: one hex digit stands for exactly four bits, a nibble. So a whole byte is always two hex digits.
To convert binary to hex, split the byte into two nibbles. One zero one one is eleven, which is B. Zero one zero one is five. So it's B five.
Programmers love hex because it's shorter and much easier to read than long strings of ones and zeros. But inside, the computer still stores binary.

Now text. Each character, a letter, digit, space or symbol, is given a number by a character set, and that number is stored in binary.
The best known is ASCII. Capital A is sixty five, B is sixty six, and so on. Lower case a is ninety seven, exactly thirty two more.

ASCII uses one byte per character, so the word Enniskillen, eleven letters, takes eleven bytes, or eighty eight bits.

That leads us to data types, another part of the new curriculum. A data type tells the computer what kind of value it's storing and how to store it.
An integer is a whole number, stored as a binary number. A float is a number with a decimal point. At GCSE you'll call that a real number.
A string is text, stored as a list of character codes, one after another. And a Boolean is just true or false, so it only needs one bit.
Here's a sneaky one. The integer seven is stored as the binary number seven. But the character seven in a string is stored as its ASCII code, fifty five.
And phone numbers should be strings, because an integer would lose the leading zero.
On to images. A bitmap image is a grid of tiny squares called pixels, and each pixel's colour is stored in binary.
Colour depth is the number of bits per pixel. One bit gives two colours, eight bits give two hundred and fifty six, and twenty four bits give over sixteen million.
Resolution is the number of pixels, width times height. More pixels means more detail, but a bigger file.
The formula: file size in bits equals width times height times colour depth. Then divide by eight for bytes.
So a ten by ten emoji with four colours. Four colours need two bits. Ten times ten times two is two hundred bits, divided by eight is twenty five bytes.
And if you double the width and the height, there are four times as many pixels, so the file is four times bigger.
Now sound. Sound is an analogue wave, smooth and continuous. To store it, the computer measures, or samples, the wave at regular intervals.
The sample rate is how many samples are taken every second, measured in hertz. CD quality is forty four thousand one hundred hertz.
The bit depth is how many bits store each sample. CDs use sixteen bits, which gives sixty five thousand five hundred and thirty six levels.
Higher sample rate or bit depth means better quality but bigger files.
File size in bits is sample rate times bit depth times the number of channels times the length in seconds. Remember stereo is two channels, and change minutes to seconds.
Which is why we need our last idea: compression, making files smaller so they take less space and download faster.
Lossless compression keeps every single bit, so you get back exactly the original. Zip files, png and gif images are lossless.
A simple lossless method is run-length encoding. Six white pixels, three black, four white becomes six W, three B, four W.
Lossy compression goes further. It throws away detail you probably won't notice, so files are much smaller, but that data is gone for ever. Think jpeg, mp3 and mp4.
A three-minute song as a CD-quality wav file is about thirty megabytes. As an mp3 it's under three. About eleven times smaller.
But never use lossy compression on a spreadsheet or a program. Lose one bit and a mark changes or the program crashes.
Let's recap. Computers use binary because transistors are switches that are on or off, and n bits give two to the power n patterns.
Binary place values are one hundred and twenty eight down to one. Add the columns with a one, or use the subtraction method to go back.
In binary addition, one plus one is zero carry one, and an answer too big for the bits is an overflow.
Each unit from kilobyte to terabyte is one thousand and twenty four of the one before, and hex is a short way of writing binary, one digit per nibble.
Integers, floats, strings and Booleans are each stored differently, and text uses character codes like ASCII and Unicode.
Image size is width times height times colour depth; sound size is sample rate times bit depth times channels times seconds. And compression is lossy or lossless.
